extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations; corporate/community relations managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, implementing, and evaluating organizational community relations programs that communicate with geographic communities and publics. Covers objectives, activity types, team composition, publics identification, and contingency factors affecting program choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive vs. Instrumental Activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities are either 'expressive' (to promote the organization and show goodwill) or 'instrumental' (to improve the community or change it to make it easier for the organization to work there).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressive examples: team visits to hospitals, open houses, sponsorships. Instrumental examples: executive speeches to Rotary, seminars, urban renewal investments. Programs may combine both; asymmetric two-way programs may supplement instrumental attempts to persuade with expressive activities to soften persuasion (e.g., sponsor a concert while lobbying leaders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model alignment of activities (public-relations models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Community relations activities should be consistent with the PR model used: press agent/publicity, public-information, two-way asymmetric, or two-way symmetric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press-agent/publicity and public-information models tend toward expressive activities (open houses, tours, sponsorships). Two-way asymmetric and two-way symmetric models stress instrumental activities (dialogue sessions, leader interviews), though asymmetric programs may add expressive activities to aid persuasion. Two-way symmetric activities are identified as most effective for meeting community relations objectives in later discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of organization and environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Community relations should reflect the interdependence between an organization and its local community; programs are 'planned, active, and continuing participation with and within a community, to maintain and enhance its environment to the benefit of both the institution and the community.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the organization's payroll, taxes, and contributions affect the community and how community goodwill, local regulations, and services affect the organization. Use this interdependence to justify program goals and activities (e.g., lobbying, philanthropy, employee involvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication objective as primary CR objective
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental objective of community relations is the communication objective: to sense how customers and community members perceive the organization and to provide timely information (two-way communication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Block's list: sense customer perceptions of service and the whole business; stay on top of complaints; involve employees in representing the company to the public; provide timely local information. Do not assume immediate attitude or behavior change is required; process and face-to-face communication are important indexes of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectations for attitude/behavior objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations may expect long-term changes in community attitudes/behaviors that benefit them, but the reasonableness depends on community nature and publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect to 'sell everyone' or convert all citizens; measure success also by process indicators (personal contact, information flow). Champion International lists desired benefits (fair taxes, open forum, nonarbitrary rules, labor pool, goodwill, early-warning information) as reasonable long-term outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community publics identification (Champion International list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify community publics such as: 'Our employees and their families; Local news media; Community opinion molders and thought leaders; Elective and other governmental officials; Local business, civic, and service organizations; Advocacy or special-interest groups; The public at large; Our customers, if any have a presence in the plant area.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this explicit list to target messages and activities; tailor different tactics for each public (e.g., media relations for press, dialogues for leaders, educational programs for residents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational linkage framework for publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Publics can be conceptualized by organizational linkages: enabling (local government), functional (employees/customers), normative (other local organizations), and diffused (activist publics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map community publics to these linkages to prioritize outreach and objectives. Example: enabling linkage (key officials) for policy/regulatory goals; functional linkage for service/employee relations; diffused linkage for activist monitoring and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team composition for community relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Community relations teams often consist of both managerial and nonmanagerial employees (not just PR specialists) who volunteer; a public relations specialist trains, assists, and evaluates the teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams may be one per small community or multiple in large metro areas. Use volunteers from across the organization to involve employees in local representation; provide training and centralized coordination from PR staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local media relations as a core activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Local community relations teams should handle local media relations because headquarters cannot manage media in thousands of communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams should develop relationships with local reporters, pitch coverage of community projects and issues, and coordinate local releases consistent with corporate messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee communication activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use internal communications (employee newsletters, highlighting employee activities) to inform staff about community engagement and to encourage participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employee newsletters should report team activities, what employees are doing in the community, and local problems. Use internal channels to build pride and involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community presentations and talks
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange company talks to civic groups, business clubs, schools, and other organizations to disseminate information and build relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a speakers' bureau, coordinate executive speeches, and tailor messages to local interests and the PR model chosen (informational vs. persuasive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Company-sponsored memberships and participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Company pays dues/expenses for employee-sponsored memberships in key local organizations and encourages employee volunteerism in community activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsorship of memberships helps build network ties and normative linkages; encourage employee civic participation and recognize contributions (awards, leaves for public office).

rubrics_metrics.name: Events, exhibits, open houses, tours, and displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponsor exhibits, open houses, tours, and film showings to disseminate information about the company to residents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these expressive/public-information tactics to shape local perceptions, especially in communities with limited prior exposure to the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation in community activities and volunteerism
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage teams and all employees to volunteer and participate in community events (cleanup drives, fund-raisers, parades).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employee involvement both supports community needs and signals organizational commitment; track participation and outcomes to demonstrate impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue sessions with community leaders and groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Invite community leaders to group sessions to discuss company performance and community problems; these are two-way activities that can be symmetric or asymmetric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue for listening, reputation sensing, and co-learning in two-way symmetric models; use for persuasion in asymmetric contexts but consider supplementing with expressive gestures to soften persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community leader interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Teams should compile lists of important community leaders and conduct personal interviews with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews provide in-depth intelligence on community concerns and influential actors; use findings to set priorities and early-warning monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: White paper for plant moves or major facility changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a white paper explaining the reasons, timing, and impacts when moving a plant or building a new facility; base it on a comprehensive sociological and political audit of the area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute to employees, community leaders, media, and elected officials to preempt misinformation and frame the decision; use as part of an instrumental community relations strategy when community impact is large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-involvement projects (philanthropy, training, coalitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage in corporate philanthropy, employee volunteer programs, political/civic activities, rebuilding urban centers, summer jobs, job training, support for elderly/minority businesses, civic center planning, or loaning staff to public agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These projects are instrumental activities that address community needs and build longer-term goodwill and structural benefits (better schools, reduced crime). Consider coalition-building for large-scale urban projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of community 'climate' studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct annual community 'climate' studies to identify local problems and community needs (e.g., Ford committees' practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use climate studies to inform program priorities, detect issues early, and tailor strategies to local conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program contingency on community structure/pluralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Community relations programs should be contingent upon the degree to which a community is centralized (power elite) or pluralistic—programs must differ for different kinds of communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess community characteristics (population size, ethnic diversity, in-migration, economic diversity, absentee-owned firms, presence of reform government) to determine whether to target centralized elites or multiple publics; more pluralistic communities require broader, multi-public approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired organizational benefits from community relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected benefits include fair, nondiscriminatory taxes; open forum in local government; nonarbitrary local rules; a ready pool of eager workers; a bankable amount of goodwill; and early-warning information on community developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these listed benefits as long-term objectives to evaluate program effectiveness beyond immediate communication outcomes; measure where feasible (e.g., regulatory outcomes, recruitment statistics, goodwill indicators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and evaluation via research/audit
rubrics_metrics.description: Use methods such as the communication audit, membership surveys, leader interviews, and message accuracy checks to evaluate how different publics receive and interpret organizational messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Grunig's study using news items asked respondents if they had heard items and what they heard to assess accuracy across publics; use multi-method evaluation to compare effectiveness of expressive vs. two-way symmetric activities.
